problem: 'he murmured' follows Carter's speech; the listener cannot tell the speaker is Mason (the wounded man) rather than Carter.
new_text: "She bit me," Mason murmured. "She savaged me like a tigress, when Rochester got the knife from her."

problem: The same opening is called 'a door in the wall' and then 'the gate' in consecutive sentences, which reads as two different openings.
new_text: This done, he walked slowly and abstractedly toward a door in the wall bordering the orchard. I, thinking he was done with me, turned to go back to the house; but I heard him call "Jane!" He had opened the door and stood waiting for me.

problem: 'John's wife and John himself' comes right after the news of Mr. John Reed's death; a reader can mistake this for John Reed. These are the Thornfield servants.
new_text: "Yes; and I will do it now." Having directed him to the servants' hall and recommended him to the care of John the manservant and his wife, I went to find Mr. Rochester.

problem: 'Robert and his sister played quietly in a corner' reads as Robert Leaven (the coachman, just arrived with Jane); it means Bessie's little son Robert. Two paragraphs later 'Robert came in' is the father, adding confusion.
new_text: I reached the lodge at Gateshead about five o'clock on the afternoon of May the first. I stopped in there before going up to the hall. It was very clean and neat: the decorative windows hung with little white curtains; the floor spotless; the grate and fire-irons polished bright; the fire burning clear. Bessie sat by the hearth, nursing her youngest child, and little Robert and his sister played quietly in a corner.

problem: 'Cairngorm eye' is obscure (a Cairngorm is a smoky Scottish quartz); most readers will not understand the image.
new_text: In each sister there was one trait of the mother, and only one: the thin, pale elder daughter had her parent's hard, stony eye, like a pebble of Cairngorm quartz; the blooming, ample younger girl had her contour of jaw and chin—perhaps slightly softened, but still giving an indefinable hardness to a face otherwise so full and handsome.

problem: 'He would send for the baby' reads as habitual action rather than 'insisted on'; 'shut up part of the house, or let it' uses 'let' (rent out), which reads as 'allow'.
new_text: "I had a dislike for her mother always; she was my husband's only sister, and a great favourite of his. He opposed the family's disowning her when she made her low marriage; and when news came of her death, he wept like a fool. He insisted on sending for the baby, though I begged him to put it out to nurse and pay for its care. I hated it the first time I laid eyes on it—a sickly, whining, pining thing! It would wail in its cradle all night—not screaming heartily like any other child, but whimpering and moaning. Reed pitied it; he used to hold it and fuss over it as if it were his own—more, indeed, than he ever noticed his own children at that age. He tried to make my children friendly to the little beggar; the darlings couldn't stand it, and he was angry with them when they showed their dislike. In his last illness he had it brought constantly to his bedside; and barely an hour before he died, he bound me with a vow to keep the creature. I would as soon have been charged with a pauper's brat from the workhouse—but he was weak, naturally weak. John does not resemble his father at all, and I am glad of it: John is like me and like my brothers—he is a true Gibson. Oh, I wish he would stop tormenting me with letters begging for money! I have no more money to give him: we are growing poor. I must dismiss half the servants and shut up part of the house, or rent it out. I can never submit to that—yet how are we to manage? Two thirds of my income goes to pay mortgage interest. John gambles terribly, and always loses—poor boy! He is surrounded by swindlers. John is ruined and degraded—his appearance is frightful—I feel ashamed for him when I see him."

problem: Eliza's answer "The Rubric" is unexplained; modern readers will not know it means the prayer book's rules for conducting services.
new_text: Eliza still said little: she clearly had no time for talk. I never saw a busier person, yet it was hard to say what she accomplished. She had an alarm clock to wake her early. What she did before breakfast I never discovered, but after that meal she divided her day into precise portions, each hour assigned its task. Three times a day she studied a little book which, on inspection, I found was a Book of Common Prayer. I asked her once what she found so compelling in it, and she said, "The Rubric"—its rules for the order of services. Three hours she spent stitching a gold-thread border on a square of crimson cloth, nearly large enough for a carpet. When I asked what it was for, she told me it was a covering for the altar of a new church recently built near Gateshead. Two hours she gave to her diary; two to working alone in the kitchen garden; and one to managing her accounts. She seemed to want no company and no conversation. I believe she was happy in her way: this routine was enough for her, and nothing annoyed her more than any event that forced her to break its clockwork regularity.

problem: Eliza's reply is in quotation marks but in reported third person ('Georgiana and she', 'she, Eliza, would go hers'), which is confusing to read and especially to hear aloud as direct speech.
new_text: "Of course not. Georgiana and I have nothing in common; we never have. I would not be burdened with her company for any consideration. Georgiana should go her own way; and I, Eliza, will go mine."

problem: Inside Georgiana's quoted words, 'if she could just get away' refers to Georgiana herself; as direct speech it sounds like she means someone else (the aunt).
new_text: Georgiana, when not pouring out her heart to me, spent most of her time lying on the sofa, complaining about the dullness of the house, and wishing again and again that her aunt Gibson would invite her to London. "It would be so much better," she said, "if I could just get away for a month or two, until all was over." I did not ask what she meant by "all being over," but I suppose she referred to her mother's expected death and the gloomy business of the funeral. Eliza generally took no more notice of her sister's laziness and complaints than if no such whining, lounging figure were there at all. One day, however, as she put away her account book and unfolded her embroidery, she suddenly rounded on her—

problem: 'here were two natures made, the one ... and the other ..., for the lack of it' is tangled; 'made ... for the lack of it' is hard to parse on first reading or hearing.
new_text: True, generous feeling counts for little with some people; but here were two natures—the one unbearably bitter, the other contemptibly bland—made so by the lack of it. Feeling without judgment is a watery drink indeed; but judgment without feeling is too harsh and dry a morsel for anyone to swallow.

problem: 'They came to tell us' has no clear referent (the nurse and Bessie? the daughters just mentioned?). Also 'a grating anguish for her woes, not my loss' is compressed and hard to follow aloud.
new_text: The nurse came in, and Bessie followed. I stayed another half hour, hoping to see some sign of softening; but she gave none. She was sinking rapidly into stupor; her mind did not rally again. At midnight she died. I was not there to close her eyes, nor were either of her daughters. Word was brought to us the next morning that it was over. By then she had been laid out. Eliza and I went to see her; Georgiana, who had burst into loud weeping, said she dared not go. There lay Sarah Reed's once robust and active body, rigid and still: her flint-like eye was shut beneath its cold lid; her brow and strong features still bore the stamp of her unyielding soul. A strange and solemn sight she was to me. I gazed at her with gloom and pain: nothing soft, nothing sweet, nothing pitying, or hopeful, or subduing did the spectacle inspire—only a grating anguish for her woes (not for any loss of mine), and a sombre, tearless dread at the fearfulness of death in such a form.

problem: The paragraph deliberately shifts to present tense, but 'I passed a tall briar' slips back into past tense mid-sequence, which jars.
new_text: They are making hay, too, in the Thornfield meadows; or rather, the labourers are just finishing their work, heading home with rakes on their shoulders, now, at the hour I arrive. I have only a field or two to cross, and then I shall reach the road and the gates. How full of roses the hedges are! But I have no time to gather any; I want to reach the house. I pass a tall briar shooting leafy, flowering branches across the path; I see the narrow stile with stone steps; and I see—Mr. Rochester sitting there, a book and a pencil in his hand. He is writing.

problem: 'It doesn't matter if I knew twenty ways' mixes tenses awkwardly within the present-tense passage.
new_text: Well, he is not a ghost; yet every nerve in my body has come unstrung. For a moment I am beyond my own control. What does this mean? I did not think I would tremble like this when I saw him, or lose my voice or the power of movement in his presence. I will go back as soon as I can move; I need not make an absolute fool of myself. I know another way to the house. It would not matter if I knew twenty ways; for he has seen me.
